Look at layout, size, switch feel if it's mechanical, and whether you need it to be wired, backlit or portable. Typing on it in a store, if you can, beats guessing from a photo. I won't quote prices that may be out of date.

topics.title: Buying a game console
topics.desc: Pick a console based on the games you actually want, who you'll play with, and your budget, including a TV or monitor, extra controllers and a storage plan. Compare exclusive games, online fees, disc versus digital, and whether friends are already on that platform. I won't invent sale prices; tell me your budget and favorite games and I can help you think it through.

topics.title: Buying everyday shoes
topics.desc: For everyday shoes, start with your budget, the weather you deal with, and how much you'll walk. Look for a fit with a little room at the toes, a secure heel, and a sole that isn't too slippery. Try them on later in the day when feet are a bit bigger, and walk around the store. I won't guess current prices.

topics.title: Buying running shoes
topics.desc: Running shoes should match your budget and the surface you'll run on. Look for a secure, comfortable fit and enough room in the toe box, and replace them when the midsole feels packed out or worn. A running shop that watches you walk or jog can help more than a guess from ads. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying a backpack
topics.desc: Decide your budget and what you'll carry: laptop, binders or gym clothes. Look for padded straps, a laptop sleeve if you need one, a fit that sits on your hips more than your neck, and zippers that feel sturdy. Try it on with some weight if you can. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying a desk
topics.desc: Measure the space, the chair and the path through the door before you buy a desk, and set a budget. Look at height, width, depth for a monitor, and storage. A desk that's too tall or too shallow will feel bad every day. I won't guess prices; tell me your budget and room size if you want help narrowing features.

topics.title: Buying a TV
topics.desc: Start with your budget, how far you sit, and whether you care most about sports, movies or a game console. Look at size, a simple picture quality comparison, HDMI ports, and the inputs you'll actually use. Sit at your usual distance if you can see it in a store. I won't invent current prices.

topics.title: Buying a used phone
topics.desc: If you're buying used, set a budget and confirm the model, storage, battery health and that the phone is unpaid and not stolen, with a trusted seller or a store policy. Test the buttons, cameras, speakers and Wi-Fi before you pay, and ask whether it can still get software updates. I won't guess street prices.

topics.title: Buying a tablet
topics.desc: A tablet is handy for reading, video and some homework, but it may not replace a laptop if you write a lot. Decide your budget, screen size, storage and whether you need a keyboard. Check if the apps you need actually work well on it. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying a mouse
topics.desc: Choose a mouse based on your budget, hand size and whether you need it for school work, games or both. Look at a comfortable shape, a reliable sensor, wired versus wireless, and whether the buttons are easy to reach. Try it if you can. I won't quote prices.

topics.title: Buying earbuds
topics.desc: Earbuds should stay in your ears comfortably and match your budget and phone. Look at fit, a secure case, battery life, and whether you want a mic or noise control. A model that stays put on a walk matters more than extra features you won't use. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying a power bank
topics.desc: A power bank is a portable charger. Pick a budget, then look at capacity, the ports your phone uses, and airline rules if you'll fly with it. A well-known brand with safety certifications is worth paying attention to. I won't guess prices or exact capacities you should buy without knowing your phone.

topics.title: Buying a router
topics.desc: A router sends Wi-Fi through your home. Match it to your budget, internet plan and the size of the place, and look at current Wi-Fi standards, coverage and easy parental or guest controls if you need them. Your internet provider may already include one. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying a winter coat
topics.desc: Pick a coat for your budget, the coldest weather you actually face, and whether you need it to stay dry in snow or rain. Look at fit over a sweater, a closable collar or hood, and pockets you'll use. Try it on and move your arms. I won't guess current prices.

topics.title: Buying a used laptop
topics.desc: For a used laptop, set a budget and check the age, storage, RAM, battery health, keyboard and screen, and whether it still gets security updates. Ask for the original charger, test it in person, and avoid a deal that seems hidden or rushed. I won't invent resale prices.

topics.title: Buying a game controller
topics.desc: Choose a controller that works with your console or PC, fits your hands, and matches your budget. Look at genuine compatibility, a solid analog stick feel, and a warranty or return option in case of stick drift. Official and well-reviewed third-party pads can both be fine. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Going for a walk
topics.desc: A walk doesn't have to be long to help. Pick a safe route, wear shoes you can actually walk in, and tell someone if you're going farther than around the block. Notice one thing along the way, and bring water if it will be more than a short loop.

topics.title: A neighborhood bike ride
topics.desc: Ride a bike that's the right size, wear a helmet, and follow the same road rules as you would on a busier street: lights if it's dim, and hand signals when you can. Stick to a route you know if you're going out alone, and lock the bike if you stop.

topics.title: Planning a picnic
topics.desc: Keep a picnic simple: something to sit on, water, food that travels well, and a bag for trash. Check the weather and park rules, and pick a public spot you can get to safely. You don't need a huge spread for it to count.

topics.title: Visiting a park
topics.desc: A park visit can be a walk, a bench and a snack, or a game of catch. Check hours, bring water, and leave the place as tidy as you found it. If you're going alone, stay in well-used areas and tell someone where you are.

topics.title: A short hike
topics.desc: For a short hike, pick a marked trail that matches your fitness, tell someone the plan, and bring water, a phone and a layer in case the weather turns. Stay on the trail, and turn around early enough to get back in daylight. You don't need a huge backpack for a short loop.

topics.title: A photo walk
topics.desc: A photo walk is just walking with a camera or phone and looking for interesting light, textures or small details. Pick a neighborhood or park, give yourself a loose theme like “circles” or “blue things,” and don't block a sidewalk to get a shot. You can do this in 20 minutes.

topics.title: Watching a sunset
topics.desc: To watch a sunset, check about when the sun will go down, pick a west-facing spot with a clear view, and arrive a little early. Bring a layer because it cools off fast. Stay aware of traffic and your way home if it will be dark after.

topics.title: Looking at the stars
topics.desc: Stars show up better away from bright lights, after your eyes adjust for a few minutes. A free sky app can help you name a few bright ones, but you don't need it. Dress warmer than you think, and stay in a place you know is safe at night.

topics.title: A scavenger hunt
topics.desc: A scavenger hunt is a list of things to find or photograph, like something red, a leaf with interesting edges, or a kind street sign. Write 8 to 12 items, set a time limit, and agree on the area and rules. It's an easy way to make a walk with a friend more fun.

topics.title: Playing catch
topics.desc: Playing catch only needs a ball and a little open space away from windows and streets. Start close, agree on how hard you'll throw, and watch the area behind your partner. Move farther apart once you're both warmed up.

topics.title: Shooting hoops at a park
topics.desc: A park hoop is an easy way to move around, even if you only take turns shooting. Bring a ball if the court might not have one, wait your turn if others are running a game, and be decent about sharing the court. Water and a break in the heat help.

topics.title: Building a snowman
topics.desc: Roll a packed base, then a smaller middle and a head, and stack them on fairly level snow. Pack the joints so the head doesn't slide, and use sticks, stones or a hat only if you're allowed to and you pick them up later. Dress for wet and cold, and watch for ice underfoot.

topics.title: Going to a farmers market
topics.desc: A farmers market is a place to walk, look at produce and sometimes hear music, even if you only buy a snack. Bring a bag and a little cash or a card if you plan to purchase something, and ask before you taste. Go early or later if you want it less crowded.

topics.title: Exploring your neighborhood
topics.desc: Pick a direction you don't usually walk, stay on public sidewalks, and notice one new street, shop or tree. Bring a charged phone, and tell someone if you'll be gone more than a short loop. You don't need a plan beyond “turn left at the end of the block and loop back.”

topics.title: Reading outside
topics.desc: Reading outside works well on a bench or a stoop with a book or your phone in shade, so the screen isn't washed out. Bring a layer, something to drink, and a way to keep pages from blowing around. Pick a public spot you feel comfortable in.

topics.title: Drawing outside
topics.desc: A small notebook and a pencil are enough for drawing outside. Pick a simple subject, like a cup, a tree or a doorway, and spend ten minutes on shapes before details. Don't block a path, and go inside if the weather turns.

topics.title: Skipping stones
topics.desc: A good skipping stone is fairly flat, and you throw it low and sidearm so it spins and kisses the water. Stand somewhere you have space and a safe backswing, and don't throw if people or animals are in the way. It takes a few tries.

topics.title: Geocaching
topics.desc: Geocaching is an outdoor scavenger hunt that uses a map or an official app to find hidden containers. Follow the listing's rules, put things back as you found them, and stay off private property. It's more fun with a friend, and you should tell someone where you're going.

topics.title: Flying a kite
topics.desc: Kites need open space away from streets, power lines and airports, plus enough wind to lift them without knocking you over. Let the line out gradually, and don't fly in a thunderstorm. A simple diamond kite is enough to start.

topics.title: Rainy-day indoor activities
topics.desc: On a rainy day you can cook something simple, organize a drawer, draw, write, play a board or video game, or watch a movie with a friend online. Set a short timer and pick one thing so the day doesn't just disappear. If you're stir-crazy, stretch or walk around the house between activities.

topics.title: Things to do with a friend when you're bored
topics.desc: When you're both bored, pick something with a clear start: a walk, a catch session, a co-op game, a photo hunt, cooking a simple snack, or working on a project together. Agree on a time so it doesn't stall. If plans fall through, have a backup that works at home.

topics.title: Things to do alone when you're bored
topics.desc: When you're alone and bored, try a short walk, a playlist and a tidy-up, a chapter of a book, a game you actually enjoy, practicing a skill for 15 minutes, or writing down a list of things you might want later. You don't have to be productive the whole time, but choosing one thing beats scrolling by default.

topics.title: A backyard game
topics.desc: A backyard or driveway game can be catch, HORSE, a beanbag toss, or a simple made-up rule game with a ball. Check you have space away from windows and streets, and agree on the rules before the first throw. It can last 10 minutes and still reset the afternoon.

topics.title: Visiting a museum
topics.desc: A museum is a low-pressure place to walk and look. Check hours, student or free times, and bag rules before you go. You don't have to read every label; pick a few rooms and one object that actually interests you.

topics.title: Respecting wildlife at a park
topics.desc: At a park, watch animals from a distance, don't feed them human food, and keep dogs where the rules say. Feeding ducks bread can make them sick, and getting close for a photo can stress the animal. Leave nests, burrows and babies alone.

topics.title: Choosing a difficulty level
topics.desc: Pick a difficulty you can learn on, not the one that just looks impressive. If every fight is a wall, drop it a step and turn it up later. If you're bored, raise it or add a personal rule. The “right” setting is the one where you still want to play tomorrow.

topics.title: Being a good teammate
topics.desc: A good teammate communicates clearly, doesn't blame people for one mistake, and plays the objective you all agreed on. Call out useful info, ping if that's easier, and say “nice” when someone does well. If you're tilted, take a breath or a short break instead of dumping it on the squad.

topics.title: Dealing with a toxic teammate
topics.desc: If a teammate is being cruel, mute or report them with the in-game tools and stop feeding the argument. You don't have to stay in voice chat. If it crosses into threats or targeted harassment, leave the match if you can and tell a trusted adult.

topics.title: Taking a break from a game
topics.desc: If a game is making you angry, you can't focus, or it's eating the time you needed for sleep or school, step away for a bit. Save if you can, close it, and do something physical or offline even for ten minutes. Coming back later with a clearer head usually beats forcing one more match.

topics.title: Learning a new game
topics.desc: When you pick up a new game, play the tutorial, try the lowest-stakes mode, and learn one system at a time instead of reading everything at once. It's fine to die or lose a lot at first. A short “beginner” video can help after you've tried it yourself.

topics.title: Using a walkthrough
topics.desc: A walkthrough is useful when you're stuck, but it can spoil surprises. Try a hint or a specific puzzle first instead of a full story guide. If you use a guide, jump to the part you need and stop when you're unstuck so the rest of the game stays yours.

topics.title: Boss fights
topics.desc: In a boss fight, watch the attack pattern before you rush in, use the space you have, and don't empty every resource on the first phase if you can help it. Take a short break if you've failed many times in a row. A specific tip for that boss is fair to look up after a real try.

topics.title: Inventory management
topics.desc: Inventory management means deciding what to keep, stack or drop so you can still pick up what you need. Store extra at a stash or vendor when the game allows it, and don't hoard a dozen almost-the-same items. A little cleanup after a mission saves you from being full at a bad time.

topics.title: Side quests
topics.desc: A side quest is an extra task that isn't required to finish the main story. Do a few if they look fun or give a useful reward, and skip them if you're tired of the game or want to see the ending. You can always come back later if the game lets you.

topics.title: New Game Plus
topics.desc: New Game Plus is a mode that lets you start the story again with some of your progress, gear or levels still intact. It's meant for a second run, often with harder enemies. Finish the first playthrough and read what that game actually carries over, because it isn't the same in every title.

topics.title: Party chat with friends
topics.desc: Party or group chat lets you talk with friends while you play, often in the console, PC or phone app. Use a headset, mute when there's loud background noise, and don't share personal details in a party with people you just met. If the chat is being ugly, you can leave.

topics.title: When a game makes you tilt
topics.desc: Tilt means you're playing worse because you're angry. After a bad loss, pause: get a drink, stretch, or stop the session. Complaining at teammates usually makes the next game worse. It's a normal feeling, and stepping away is a real strategy, not quitting forever.

topics.title: Picking a class or character
topics.desc: Pick a class or character that matches how you like to play: up close, from a distance, or supporting others. Try one in a training or low-stakes mode before you buy a lot of upgrades. You can often switch later, so you don't have to lock in a “main” on day one.

topics.title: Reading a skill tree
topics.desc: A skill tree is a map of upgrades. Read what a node actually does, then spend points on a plan that supports how you already play, instead of grabbing every bright icon. You can often respec later. If you're stuck, look up that game's reset rules, not a random “best build” you can't use yet.

topics.title: Co-op games
topics.desc: A co-op game is made for people to play together toward the same goal, not against each other. Agree on the difficulty, who leads, and how long you'll play. Patience matters more than being the best, especially if one of you is new.

topics.title: Speedrunning basics
topics.desc: Speedrunning is trying to finish a game, or a part of it, as quickly as you can under agreed rules. Start by learning a clean route, then shave time once you're consistent. Watch a beginner's run, not only world records, and don't wreck a file you care about.

topics.title: Completion and collectibles
topics.desc: Going for completion means finding collectibles or finishing every side activity. It can be satisfying, or it can burn you out. If you're tired, stop, enjoy the ending, and come back later with a checklist only if you still want to. The game is allowed to be finished at 60 percent.

topics.title: Asking for an extension
topics.desc: If you need more time on an assignment, ask before the deadline when you can. Email or tell your teacher clearly: the assignment name, why you need more time, and a realistic date you can turn it in. Be honest, and have a plan to finish, because an extension is a request, not a guarantee.

topics.title: Studying with a classmate
topics.desc: Studying with a classmate works if you set a goal, like reviewing a chapter or quizzing each other, and a time limit. Take turns explaining, and don't only copy answers. If you start just chatting, take a short break, then come back to the list.

topics.title: Breaking down a long project
topics.desc: Split a long project into pieces with their own due dates: research, outline, first draft, and a final pass. Start with the part that unlocks the rest, and put those mini-deadlines on a calendar. A little work several days in a row beats one all-nighter.

topics.title: Math word problems
topics.desc: For a word problem, read it twice, underline what it's asking, and list the numbers and units you have. Write an equation or a picture before you calculate, then check that the answer's units and size make sense. If you're stuck, try a simpler example with smaller numbers first.

topics.title: Studying for a quiz tomorrow
topics.desc: If the quiz is tomorrow, focus on the main ideas, formulas or terms your teacher emphasized, not a perfect reread of everything. Make a short list, test yourself out loud or on paper, sleep enough, and do a quick review in the morning. Don't stay up so late that you can't think.

topics.title: When you missed class
topics.desc: If you missed class, get the notes and any handouts from a classmate or the class page, then ask the teacher what you should prioritize, not “did I miss anything?” Do the work as soon as you can so the next lesson isn't a pile-on.

topics.title: Organizing a binder
topics.desc: Use a binder with a simple system: one tab per class, newest papers in a consistent place, and a pocket for things that still need to go home. Once a week, take out junk and file what's left. A messy binder costs you more time than the few minutes of sorting.

topics.title: Writing a lab report
topics.desc: A lab report usually has a purpose, method, data, and a conclusion that answers the question using your results. Write the steps so someone else could repeat them, put the data in a table or graph if you can, and don't change numbers to look “right.” Follow your teacher's required headings.

topics.title: Reading a textbook chapter
topics.desc: For a textbook chapter, skim headings and the summary first, then read a section at a time and write a few questions or notes in your own words. Don't highlight everything. If a paragraph is dense, slow down and work an example before you move on.

topics.title: Memorizing a speech
topics.desc: Memorize a speech in chunks, out loud, and practice the transitions between chunks more than any single sentence. Recite it without the paper, then check where you stumble and practice those spots. A few shorter practices beat one exhausted run the night before.

topics.title: Estimating your grade
topics.desc: To estimate a grade, list each graded item, its score, and its weight, then add the weighted pieces. If you don't have weights, use the syllabus or ask the teacher. A grade calculator or a simple spreadsheet can help, but the syllabus is the source of truth.

topics.title: When you don't understand the homework
topics.desc: If you don't understand the homework, try the directions and one example from class first, then try a short official explanation or your notes. Write down exactly where you got stuck and ask the teacher, a tutor or a classmate that specific question. Don't copy a finished answer just to be done.

topics.title: Citing a website
topics.desc: To cite a website, you usually need the author if there is one, the title, the site name, the date you accessed it, and the URL, in the style your teacher asked for, such as MLA or APA. If no author is listed, start with the title. When you're unsure, cite it anyway.

topics.title: Talking to a school counselor
topics.desc: A school counselor can help with classes, college or job plans, and also with stress or problems at school. You can ask a teacher or the office how to make an appointment, and you can say as much or as little as you want at first. If you're in danger or thinking of being unsafe, tell them clearly so they can help you get support.

topics.title: Choosing electives
topics.desc: Choose electives based on what you're curious about, what you might need later, and a realistic workload, not only what friends pick. Read the course description, ask a student who already took it, and leave a little room in your schedule so you aren't overloaded. You can often change it early if it's a poor fit.

topics.title: Organizing a backpack
topics.desc: Keep only what you need for the day in your backpack: binder or folders, a writing kit, charger, water and lunch if you bring it. Use the same pockets every time so keys and earbuds have a home. Empty crumbs and old papers once a week so the bag stays lighter.

topics.title: Waking up on time
topics.desc: Put the alarm across the room so you have to stand up, set it for a time you can actually live with, and start winding down at a consistent hour. Lay out clothes and pack the bag the night before so morning is shorter. If you still can't get up, talk with a parent or a doctor; it isn't always just willpower.

topics.title: Packing a lunch
topics.desc: A simple lunch is a main, a fruit or vegetable, and a drink, packed in containers that won't leak. Make it the night before if mornings are rushed, and include an ice pack if anything needs to stay cold. Leftovers and a sandwich are both fine; it doesn't have to look fancy.

topics.title: Morning routine
topics.desc: A useful morning routine is short and repeatable: get up, wash up, get dressed, eat something, grab the bag you packed, and leave with a little time to spare. Put the things you always forget by the door. You don't need a perfect aesthetic routine for it to work.

topics.title: Evening routine
topics.desc: An evening routine can be packing the bag, setting out clothes, plugging in devices, washing up, and putting the phone away so you can sleep. Start it at a regular time, even if it's only 20 minutes. The goal is a calmer morning and enough sleep, not a perfect schedule.

topics.title: Cleaning your room
topics.desc: Clean a room in passes, not all at once: trash first, then dishes and dishes-like cups, then clothes into hamper or put-away, then surfaces, then the floor. Set a timer for 15 minutes if the mess feels huge. Done-enough is better than waiting to do it perfectly.

topics.title: Taking out the trash
topics.desc: Tie or close the bag, carry it so it doesn't tear, and put it where your home actually collects trash, on the right night if you have pickup. Replace the liner if you have one, and wash your hands after. If a bag is leaking, double-bag it.

topics.title: Setting the table
topics.desc: A simple table setting is a plate, fork on the left, knife and spoon on the right with the knife blade toward the plate, and a drink above the knife. Add a napkin under the forks or to the side. For a casual meal at home, getting a plate, utensil and drink for each person is enough.

topics.title: Walking a dog
topics.desc: Use a secure leash, bring bags to clean up, and walk at a pace the dog can handle in the weather. Keep the dog away from traffic, and ask before you let it greet another dog or person. Bring water on a longer or hot walk, and don't leave a dog locked in a hot car.

topics.title: Remembering your keys
topics.desc: Give your keys a home, like a hook or a dish by the door, and put them there every time you walk in. Check for keys, phone and wallet as a set before you lock the door. A small tile or label on the keyring can help if they still go missing.

topics.title: If you get locked out
topics.desc: If you're locked out, first check other doors and whether anyone you trust is home or nearby. Call a parent, roommate or the building office before you try to force a door or window, which can be unsafe or count as breaking in. Wait in a public, well-lit place if you can, and don't share that the house is empty with strangers.

topics.title: Ordering at a counter
topics.desc: When you order at a counter, know what you want or ask a short question, then say the item clearly, including size or any change you need. Have your payment ready, check the order if they repeat it, and step aside if you need time. “Please” and “thank you” go a long way.

topics.title: Using self-checkout
topics.desc: At self-checkout, scan each item so it lands in the bagging area, enter a produce code or use the scale when the screen asks, and follow the prompts to pay. If something won't scan or you have an age-restricted item, wait for the attendant instead of guessing. Don't take unpaid items.

topics.title: Being a good guest
topics.desc: As a guest, be on time, greet the hosts, follow the house rules, and clean up after yourself. Don't go through private rooms or the fridge without asking, and say thank you when you leave. A short thank-you text later is a nice extra, not a requirement.

topics.title: When plans get canceled
topics.desc: If plans get canceled, a short “thanks for letting me know, let's find another time” is enough, even if you're disappointed. You can say you're bummered and still be civil. If you're the one canceling, tell them as soon as you know and offer another day when you can.

topics.title: Buying a new phone
topics.desc: For a new phone, start with your budget and whether you want to stay in the same app and account system you already use. Look at storage, battery life, camera needs, size in your hand, and how many years of software updates the model is expected to get. I won't invent prices; tell me your budget and I can help you think through the features.

topics.title: Buying a bike
topics.desc: A regular bike should fit your budget, your height and how you'll ride: around town, to school or on trails. Look at frame size, brake type, tire width and a shop that will help with a test ride and fit. Include a helmet and a lock in your plan. I won't guess current prices.

topics.title: Buying a skateboard
topics.desc: For a first skateboard, decide your budget and whether you want a complete board so the parts are already matched. Look at deck length for your shoe size, sturdy trucks and wheels that match street or park riding, and a helmet plus pads. A shop can help with setup. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying speakers
topics.desc: Choose speakers based on your budget, where they'll sit and whether you need Bluetooth, a plug-in aux or a computer USB connection. Listen in person if you can, and check volume needs so you don't buy something that distorts when turned up. I won't quote prices that may be out of date.

topics.title: Buying a webcam
topics.desc: A webcam should match your budget and how you'll use it: class, calls or recording. Look at a clear image in your actual lighting, a reliable mount, and whether your laptop already has a decent built-in camera. A good mic can matter as much as the picture. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying a microphone
topics.desc: Tell me your budget and whether the mic is for calls, recording or streaming. Look at USB versus other connections, a simple stand, and how it sounds on your actual computer. A quiet room often helps more than a pricey mic. I won't guess current prices.

topics.title: Buying a gaming chair
topics.desc: A gaming chair should fit your body and budget the same way an office chair does: lower-back support, adjustable height and a seat you can sit in for a while. Try it if you can, and don't assume a racing-style design is more comfortable. I won't invent prices; tell me your budget and how long you sit.

topics.title: Buying a smartwatch
topics.desc: A smartwatch only helps if you'll actually wear it. Start with your budget, your phone type, battery life and the features you'll use, like timers or activity tracking. You don't need every sensor. I won't invent prices; tell me your budget and phone and I can help you think about what matters.

topics.title: Choosing a phone plan
topics.desc: A phone plan should fit your budget and how much data you actually use, not the biggest advertised number. Compare monthly cost, hotspot or family-plan rules, coverage where you live, and contract versus prepaid. Read the fine print on fees. I won't invent plan prices.

topics.title: Buying a phone case
topics.desc: Pick a case for your exact phone model, your budget and how rough you are on a phone. Look at drop protection, whether you can reach the buttons and ports, and a fit that doesn't block the camera or charging. I won't guess prices.

topics.title: Buying a screen protector
topics.desc: A screen protector should be made for your exact phone model. Look at a clean install, a cutout that matches the speaker and camera, and whether you want glass or a thinner film. Dust under the protector is the usual problem, so follow the cleaning steps. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying a bike helmet
topics.desc: A helmet should meet a safety standard, fit level and snug, and sit straight on your head, not tipped back. Look for adjustable straps that form a V under each ear, and replace a helmet after a serious hit. Choose one you'll actually wear. I won't invent prices; tell me your budget if you want help thinking about features.

topics.title: Buying a printer
topics.desc: Start with your budget and what you'll print: homework now and then, or lots of color pages. Look at ink or toner costs over time, paper handling, and whether you need wireless printing from a phone. The cheap printer can be expensive if the ink is not. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying an external drive
topics.desc: An external drive is for extra files or backups. Choose a budget, then look at capacity, USB type, and whether you want a rugged drive if it will travel. For backups, pick something you will actually plug in on a schedule. I won't guess street prices.

topics.title: Buying a used bike
topics.desc: On a used bike, set a budget and check frame size, rust, bent wheels, brake function and that the gears shift cleanly. Take a test ride, and have a shop inspect it if you're unsure. Ask whether it was stolen. I won't invent resale prices.

topics.title: Reading product reviews
topics.desc: When you read reviews, look for recent comments from people who used the product the way you will, and be skeptical of a pile of five-star reviews that all sound the same. Photos, verified-purchase tags and a mix of ratings are more useful than a single rave or rant.

topics.title: Return policies
topics.desc: A return policy says whether you can bring an item back, how many days you have, and whether you need a receipt or the original packaging. Read it before you buy, keep the receipt, and check whether opened items or sale items are excluded. The store's written policy is what counts, not a guess.

topics.title: Warranties
topics.desc: A warranty is a promise to repair or replace a product if it fails in a stated way, for a stated time. Read what it actually covers, how long it lasts, and what voids it. An extended warranty is optional; compare the cost with what the free manufacturer warranty already includes. I won't invent prices.

topics.title: Buying school supplies
topics.desc: Make a list from the school or teacher's supply list, then buy only what you still need so you don't double up. Look for sturdy basics first: paper, pens, a binder and a bag that already works. Wait on extras until you know the class uses them. I won't invent prices; a budget helps if you tell me one.

topics.title: Force quitting a Mac app
topics.desc: If a Mac app freezes, press Option-Command-Escape, select the app, and click Force Quit. You can also Option-click the app's icon in the Dock and choose Force Quit. You'll lose unsaved work in that app, so use this when it won't respond any other way.

topics.title: Finder basics
topics.desc: Finder is how you browse files on a Mac. Open it from the smiling face icon in the Dock, then use the sidebar to reach Desktop, Documents, Downloads and drives. List, icon or column view changes how folders look, and Command-F searches.

topics.title: Spotlight on a Mac
topics.desc: Spotlight finds apps, documents and settings on a Mac. Press Command-Space, type a few letters, and press Return to open the top result. You can also do quick calculations in the same window. It's often faster than hunting through folders.

topics.title: Installing a Mac app
topics.desc: The safer way to install a Mac app is from the App Store, or from the developer's site as a .dmg or .pkg you trust. Open the installer, drag the app to Applications if that's the method, then eject the disk image. Don't install software from a random pop-up or email link.

topics.title: Uninstalling a Mac app
topics.desc: To remove a Mac app, open Finder, go to Applications, and drag the app to the Trash, then empty the Trash when you're sure. Some apps have their own uninstaller. Deleting the icon from the Dock only removes the shortcut, not the app.

topics.title: Mac keyboard shortcuts
topics.desc: On a Mac, Command is the main shortcut key: Command-C copies, Command-V pastes, Command-Z undoes, Command-S saves and Command-Q quits. Command-Tab switches apps, and Command-W closes a window. A few shortcuts can save a lot of menu hunting.

topics.title: Time Machine backups
topics.desc: Time Machine is Apple's built-in Mac backup. Connect a dedicated external drive, choose it in System Settings under Time Machine, and let it run on a schedule. Test that you can restore a file once, and don't use that drive as your only everyday storage.

topics.title: Connecting a laptop to a monitor
topics.desc: To use an external monitor, match the cable to the ports on the laptop and the display, such as HDMI or USB-C, and use an adapter if they don't match. Then choose extend or mirror in the computer's display settings and set the correct resolution. A loose cable is the usual reason nothing appears.

topics.title: The Windows Start menu
topics.desc: The Start menu is where you find apps, power options and settings on Windows. Click the Windows icon or press the Windows key, then type the name of an app to open it. You can pin apps you use often and use the power button in the menu to shut down or restart.

topics.title: Task Manager
topics.desc: Task Manager shows running programs on Windows and lets you close one that is frozen. Press Ctrl-Shift-Esc, or Ctrl-Alt-Delete and choose Task Manager, then select the app and End task. Use it when a window says not responding, and avoid ending processes you don't recognize.

topics.title: File Explorer
topics.desc: File Explorer is how you browse files on Windows. Open it from the taskbar folder icon, then use the left sidebar for This PC, Documents and Downloads. You can change the view, search in a folder, and go up one level with the back or up button.

topics.title: Installing a Windows program
topics.desc: Install Windows software from the Microsoft Store or the official site of a program you trust. Open the installer, follow the steps, and decline extra bundled offers you don't want. Don't run an installer that arrived in a surprise email or pop-up.

topics.title: Uninstalling a Windows program
topics.desc: To remove a Windows program, open Settings, then Apps, find it in the list and choose Uninstall. You can also use the older Programs and Features panel. Restart if the installer asks, and don't delete program folders by hand unless you know that's required.

topics.title: Alt+Tab
topics.desc: Alt+Tab switches between open windows on Windows. Hold Alt and press Tab to move through the list, then release on the window you want. On a Mac, Command-Tab does a similar job for apps. It's faster than hunting on the taskbar.

topics.title: Snipping a screenshot on Windows
topics.desc: On Windows, press Windows+Shift+S to open the snipping bar and drag to capture part of the screen. The shot goes to the clipboard so you can paste it, and a preview often lets you save it. The older Print Screen key can also copy the whole screen, depending on settings.

topics.title: Updating Windows
topics.desc: Windows updates fix bugs and close security holes. Open Settings, then Windows Update, and choose Check for updates. Use a power connection for a big update, save your work, and let the PC restart when it asks. Don't download Windows from a random site.

topics.title: Updating a Mac
topics.desc: On a Mac, open System Settings, then General, then Software Update, and install updates from Apple. Back up first if it's a major macOS version, plug in the power adapter, and don't close the lid mid-install. Avoid macOS installers from unofficial sites.

topics.title: Emptying Trash or Recycle Bin
topics.desc: Deleted files usually go to Trash on a Mac or the Recycle Bin on Windows, so you can restore them until you empty it. Emptying frees space and makes those files much harder to get back. Check once before you empty, especially for photos or school work.

topics.title: Safely ejecting a USB drive
topics.desc: Before you unplug a USB drive, eject it first so the computer can finish writing files. On a Mac, click the eject icon next to the drive in Finder. On Windows, use Eject from the taskbar or File Explorer, wait for the all-clear, then unplug. Pulling it out mid-copy can corrupt files.

topics.title: Printing from a computer
topics.desc: To print, open the document, choose Print, pick the correct printer, and check preview, page range and color versus black and white. Make sure the printer is on, has paper, and is connected to the same Wi-Fi or cable. A wrong printer in the list is a common miss.

topics.title: Split-screen windows
topics.desc: Split-screen lets two windows share the display. On Windows, drag a window to the left or right edge, or hold the Windows key and an arrow key. On a Mac, use the green window button and Tile, or drag if your macOS version supports it. It's handy for notes and a video at once.

topics.title: Closing a frozen Windows app
topics.desc: If a Windows app is frozen, wait a few seconds, then use the X or Alt+F4. If that fails, open Task Manager with Ctrl-Shift-Esc, select the app, and choose End task. You'll lose unsaved work in that app, so try a regular close first.

topics.title: Texting versus calling
topics.desc: Text when a short message is enough, like a time, a link or a quick yes or no. Call when the topic is long, emotional, confusing, or you need a decision right away. If you're not sure the person can talk, a text that says 'can I call?' is polite.

topics.title: Double texting
topics.desc: A second text is fine when the first one was easy to miss, or when you have a real new detail. Stacking a bunch of messages when someone hasn't replied can feel like pressure. Wait a reasonable time, and keep a follow-up short and kind.

topics.title: Tone in text messages
topics.desc: Tone is easy to misread in a text because there's no voice. Short replies can look cold, and sarcasm often falls flat. If a message could be taken two ways, add a few words or ask in person. Read it once before you send, especially if you're upset.

topics.title: Group chat etiquette
topics.desc: In a group chat, stay on the shared topic, don't call someone out in front of everyone, and take a private issue to a private thread. Mute notifications if the chat is noisy, and don't add a person without checking. A quick reply beats a long monologue.

topics.title: Asking someone to hang out by text
topics.desc: A hangout text works better when it is specific: a plan, a time and an easy out if they can't. 'Want to get food after school Thursday?' is clearer than 'we should hang out sometime.' If they say no, keep it light and don't push.

topics.title: How long to wait before replying
topics.desc: You don't owe anyone an instant reply. Answer when you can give a real response, and if you'll be slow, a short 'I'll get back to you' is enough. Repeatedly ignoring someone on purpose is different from being busy.

topics.title: Not screenshotting private chats
topics.desc: A private chat was meant for the people in it. Screenshotting and sharing it can break trust and can spread something someone never agreed to share. If you're worried about safety, tell a trusted adult instead of posting the chat. Don't forward private messages for drama.

topics.title: When not to post
topics.desc: Pause before you post if you're angry, if it involves someone else's private life, or if you wouldn't be okay with a parent, teacher or future you seeing it. A story that vanishes still can be saved. When in doubt, don't post it.

topics.title: Muting or unfollowing quietly
topics.desc: Muting, unfollowing or hiding a person's posts can be a calm way to take a break without a fight. You don't have to announce it. If the problem is bigger than a feed, a direct, kind conversation or some space may still be needed.

topics.title: A friend request from a stranger
topics.desc: You don't have to accept a friend or follow request from someone you don't know. Check whether you have friends in common, ignore anything that feels like a scam or a compliment that's too much, and never send codes, money or private photos. It's fine to decline or ignore.

topics.title: Responding to a mean comment
topics.desc: You don't have to reply to a mean comment. If you do, a short calm line or hiding the comment is often better than a long argument. If it keeps going or feels threatening, block, report it, and tell a trusted adult. Don't pile on in return.

topics.title: Not oversharing in a story
topics.desc: A story still can be screenshotted. Skip live locations, your house, when you're home alone, private family business, and anything you wouldn't say in a hallway. Share the fun part without handing a stranger your schedule.

topics.title: Emoji and tone
topics.desc: An emoji can soften a short text, but it can't fix a message that's actually unkind, and a pile of them can look messy in a serious note. Use them when they match how you talk, and skip them in something formal like an email to a teacher.

topics.title: Leaving a chat politely
topics.desc: If you need to go mid-conversation, a short 'gotta go, talk later' is enough. You don't have to explain your whole evening. In a group, you can mute and catch up later instead of vanishing mid-plan. If you made a plan, confirm it before you drop off.

topics.title: Starting a new hobby
topics.desc: To start a hobby, pick something you actually want to try, start small, and give it a few honest sessions before you buy a lot of gear. Borrow or use what you have at first, and look for one simple beginner project. It's okay if you're bad at it at the start.

topics.title: Learning guitar
topics.desc: Start with a guitar that you can hold comfortably, a tuner, and a few minutes most days rather than one long cram. Learn to tune, a couple of open chords, and a simple song you like. Buzzing strings and sore fingertips are normal at first. I can help with a practice plan; I won't invent prices for a guitar.

topics.title: Starting journaling
topics.desc: Journaling can be a few sentences about your day, a list, or one thing that's on your mind. You don't need a special notebook or a long entry every night. Keep it private, skip a day if you need to, and don't worry about writing well.

topics.title: Starting to run
topics.desc: If you're new to running, mix walking and short jogs, wear shoes that already feel okay, and start easier than you think. A little progress each week is safer than going hard on day one. Stop for sharp pain, and check with a parent or doctor if you have a health question.

topics.title: Learning a language
topics.desc: A language sticks when you practice a little often: words you actually need, short listening, and speaking out loud even if you feel silly. One app can help, but talking and reading real sentences matters too. Pick one language and a small daily habit over five at once.

topics.title: Learning to bake
topics.desc: Start with a simple recipe, measure carefully, and read the whole recipe once before you preheat the oven. Use oven mitts, keep a timer, and don't open the oven every minute. If something burns or falls, that's a normal first bake, not a sign you should quit.

topics.title: Starting gardening
topics.desc: Start small: one pot or a short row, a plant that fits your light, and a watering habit you can keep. Overwatering is a common first mistake. A seed packet or a starter plant from a local shop is enough; you don't need a huge yard. I won't invent prices for gear.

topics.title: A reading habit
topics.desc: A reading habit can start with ten quiet minutes and a book or article you actually want to finish, not only assigned ones. Keep the book where you'll see it, and it's okay to drop a book that isn't working and try another. Pages add up in small sessions.

topics.title: Learning to skateboard
topics.desc: Start on a flat, open place with a helmet, and practice standing, pushing and stopping before tricks. Fall practice and pads help. Keep sessions short at first, and don't ride in traffic or down a steep hill until you can start and stop with control.

topics.title: Starting weightlifting
topics.desc: If you're new to weights, learn a few basic movements with light load or even no weight, and ask someone who knows the form, like a coach. Rest days matter. Sharp pain is a stop sign. Check with a parent or doctor if you have a health question, and don't chase heavy numbers in week one.

topics.title: Starting yoga
topics.desc: Yoga can start with a short beginner video or class, a clear floor space, and shoes off. Move in a range that you can breathe through, and skip anything that hurts. You don't need fancy clothes. If you have an injury, ask a parent or doctor first.

topics.title: Getting into board games
topics.desc: Start with a game that has a short rulebook and a number of players you can actually gather. Learn one game well before buying a shelf of them. A library, a friend or a game cafe is a low-cost way to try something first. I won't invent game prices.

topics.title: Rest days
topics.desc: Rest days are part of training, not skipping. Muscles and joints need time to recover, especially if you're new or you just increased how hard you work. An easy walk can be fine; a rest day isn't a license to stay still all week, and it isn't a failure.

topics.title: Bodyweight exercises
topics.desc: Bodyweight moves use your own weight: squats, push-ups from the knees or toes, planks, and lunges, done with control. Start with a number you can repeat with decent form, and rest between sets. You don't need a gym. Stop if something hurts sharply.

topics.title: How to do a push-up
topics.desc: A solid push-up starts in a straight line from head to heels, hands under the shoulders, and a controlled lower and press. Knees-down or an incline on a sturdy surface is a fair way to build up. Don't let your hips sag or pike, and stop if your wrists or shoulders complain sharply.

topics.title: How to do a squat
topics.desc: In a squat, sit your hips back, keep your heels down, and keep your chest from collapsing, then stand up with control. A chair squat is a good starting point. Go only as low as you can with balance. Knee discomfort that is sharp is a stop, not something to push through.

topics.title: Starting to jog
topics.desc: A first jog can be a walk with short jogging intervals, on a route you know, in shoes that already feel comfortable. Breathe steadily, and slow to a walk when you need to. Build up over weeks, not in one afternoon. Check in with a parent or doctor if you have a health concern.

topics.title: Soreness after a workout
topics.desc: Soreness a day later can happen when you did something new, and light movement, sleep and water often help more than doing nothing all day. Sharp, sudden or joint pain is different, and swelling or pain that doesn't ease is a reason to tell a parent and, if needed, a doctor. Don't add a harder workout on top of bad pain.

topics.title: Gym basics for beginners
topics.desc: At a gym, start with a short plan, wipe equipment when you're done, and don't be afraid to ask staff how a machine works. You belong there as a beginner. Skip the heaviest weights until the movement feels familiar, and give people space. A parent or guardian may need to go with you, depending on the gym.

topics.title: When to stop a workout
topics.desc: Stop a workout for sharp pain, dizziness, chest pain, trouble breathing that feels wrong, or if you feel like you might faint. Tired is different from hurt. Tell a parent or get medical help for scary symptoms. It's smart, not weak, to stop.

topics.title: Jump rope basics
topics.desc: A jump rope should reach about mid-chest when you stand on the middle. Jump low, keep elbows close, and start with a few jumps at a time on a forgiving surface, not concrete all day. Wear shoes, and stop if your calves or shins complain sharply.

topics.title: A simple home workout
topics.desc: A simple home workout can be a short warm-up, a few bodyweight moves, and a cool-down stretch, done in a clear space. You don't need a long session. Pick a number of rounds you can finish with decent form, and rest between moves. Stop if something hurts sharply.

topics.title: Breathing during exercise
topics.desc: During exercise, try to breathe steadily instead of holding your breath, especially on strength moves: often out on the effort, in on the easier part. If you can't talk at all during an easy walk, slow down. Practice, not panic, is the goal.

topics.title: Tracking workouts
topics.desc: A simple log of what you did, how it felt, and maybe how long it took is enough. You don't need a fancy app. Tracking helps you see progress and avoid jumping too far too soon. Don't let the numbers become the only reason you move.

topics.title: Making toast
topics.desc: Toast is bread in a toaster or in a toaster oven until it's the color you like. Use a dry counter, don't use metal in a toaster, and unplug a stuck toaster before you fish anything out. Let it cool a second before you add butter so it doesn't shred the bread.

topics.title: Boxed mac and cheese
topics.desc: Boxed mac usually means boiling the pasta in a pot, draining it, then stirring in the included sauce, milk or butter as the box says. Use a timer so the pasta doesn't go mushy, and keep pot handles turned in. Read the actual box; brands differ a little.

topics.title: Cooking a frozen pizza
topics.desc: For a frozen pizza, heat the oven to the temperature on the box, put the pizza on the rack or pan it lists, and use the time range as a start, not a guess. Use oven mitts, and check that the cheese is melted and the crust isn't pale or burned. Don't put a cardboard box in the oven.

topics.title: Upgrading instant ramen
topics.desc: Instant ramen is better with the noodles cooked, then extras you already have: an egg, frozen vegetables, leftover chicken, or a little less of the seasoning packet if it's too salty. Boil safely, and don't eat dry seasoning straight from the packet as a meal.

topics.title: A simple green salad
topics.desc: A simple salad is washed greens, a few toppings you like, and a light dressing tossed just before you eat so it doesn't wilt. Dry the leaves so the dressing sticks. Leftover cooked chicken or beans can make it more of a meal.

topics.title: Pasta with jarred sauce
topics.desc: Boil pasta in salted water, start heating jarred sauce in a pan, then combine them so the sauce coats the noodles. Save a splash of pasta water if the sauce is thick. Keep pot handles in, and use a timer so the pasta isn't mushy.

topics.title: A basic smoothie
topics.desc: A basic smoothie is frozen or fresh fruit, a liquid like milk or yogurt, and a blender, blended until smooth. Don't overfill, and put the lid on. A handful of greens or nut butter is optional. Drink it soon, and wash the blender so it doesn't get sticky.

topics.title: Canned soup
topics.desc: Canned soup is heated in a pot on the stove or in a microwave-safe bowl, following the can for whether to add water. Stir so it heats evenly, and don't boil a cream soup on high until it scorches. Use a pot holder or a sleeve on a hot bowl.

topics.title: A baked potato
topics.desc: A baked potato can go in a hot oven, pierced with a fork first so steam can escape, until a knife slides in easily. Microwave is faster if you still pierce it. Use oven mitts, and add toppings after it cools a moment. Don't wrap it in foil in a microwave.

topics.title: Fried eggs
topics.desc: For a fried egg, warm a little oil or butter in a pan on medium, crack the egg in, and cook until the white is set. Cover briefly if you want the top firmer. Slide it out with a spatula, and wash your hands after handling raw egg.

topics.title: Simple tacos
topics.desc: Simple tacos can be warmed tortillas, a cooked filling like beans, leftover meat or scrambled eggs, and toppings such as cheese, salsa or lettuce. Warm the tortillas so they don't crack, and keep raw meat fully cooked before it goes in. Let everyone build their own.

topics.title: Leftover fried rice
topics.desc: Fried rice works best with leftover cold rice, a hot pan, a little oil, and mix-ins like egg, frozen vegetables or leftover cooked meat. Stir so it doesn't stick, and heat leftovers until they're hot all the way through. Freshly made sticky rice can turn gummy.

topics.title: Why leaves change color
topics.desc: Leaves look green in summer because of chlorophyll. In fall, many trees stop making as much of it, and yellow and orange colors that were already there can show, while reds often form in cooler, bright days. A brown leaf is usually done and ready to drop. Weather and the tree type both matter.

topics.title: Thunderstorm safety
topics.desc: If thunder is close, get inside a sturdy building or a hard-topped car, not under a lone tree. Stay off open fields, water and tall metal. Wait about 30 minutes after the last thunder before you go back out. A phone is safe to use indoors; a corded device and plumbing are not the first choice in a storm.

topics.title: Dressing for cold weather
topics.desc: In cold weather, layers trap heat better than one thick piece: a base layer, something warm in the middle, and a wind- or water-resistant shell if it's wet or windy. Cover head, hands and feet, and change out of wet clothes. If you feel numb, clumsy or unusually sleepy, get inside and tell an adult.

topics.title: Staying cool in a heat wave
topics.desc: In a heat wave, drink water, stay in the shade or a cool indoor place during the hottest part of the day, and wear light, loose clothes. Slow down hard exercise outdoors. Dizziness, confusion or someone who stops sweating in extreme heat is an emergency: get help and get them cool.

topics.title: Icy sidewalks
topics.desc: On ice, take short steps, keep your hands out of your pockets, and use shoes with some grip. Give yourself more time, use a railing, and test a step before you commit. Salt or sand helps where you're allowed to put it. A hard fall, especially on the head, is a reason to tell an adult.

topics.title: Tornado watch versus warning
topics.desc: A tornado watch means conditions could produce a tornado, so stay aware and know where you'd go. A warning means a tornado is happening or is about to, and you should get to a safe place right away: a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Follow official local alerts, not a rumor.

topics.title: Daylight saving time
topics.desc: Daylight saving time is when many places move clocks forward in spring and back in fall so evenings have more daylight in the warmer months. Not every place uses it, and the exact dates are set by law. The Sunday of a change can feel like a lost or gained hour of sleep, so plan extra time that morning.

topics.title: Solstices and equinoxes
topics.desc: A solstice is when the year's longest or shortest stretch of daylight happens, around June and December in the US. An equinox, around March and September, is when day and night are close to equal. They come from Earth's tilt as it orbits the Sun, not from the planet getting nearer or farther in a simple way.

topics.title: Thanksgiving
topics.desc: Thanksgiving in the United States is a late-November holiday when many people share a meal, name things they're grateful for, and spend time with family or friends. Plans and traditions differ, and not every table looks the same. If you're a guest, ask what to bring, and a simple thanks goes a long way.

topics.title: Thanksgiving leftovers
topics.desc: Leftovers should go into the fridge within about two hours of the meal, in shallow containers so they cool. Reheat until they're hot all the way through, and when in doubt, throw food that's been out too long away. A leftover sandwich or a simple plate is a classic next-day meal.

topics.title: Helping with Thanksgiving dinner
topics.desc: Help in the kitchen by asking what is actually needed: setting the table, washing bowls as they pile up, stirring something on a timer, or staying out of the way during a careful step. Wash your hands, use oven mitts, and don't taste from a shared spoon and put it back. Offers that are specific are more useful than standing in the doorway.

topics.title: Christmas basics
topics.desc: Christmas is a December holiday that many Christians celebrate as the birth of Jesus, and many other people also mark with gifts, lights, meals and time off. Traditions vary by family and culture. If you're visiting, ask about their customs, and a kind greeting is enough if you don't celebrate it yourself.

topics.title: Christmas gifts on a budget
topics.desc: A good gift can be small, handmade, useful or just thoughtful; it doesn't have to be expensive. Set a budget first, make a short list, and skip panic buying. A card with a real note still counts. I won't invent store prices; tell me a budget and who it's for and I can help you think of ideas.

topics.title: Decorating for Christmas
topics.desc: Decorations can be as simple as lights, paper, or a few ornaments, as long as they're used safely: indoor lights indoors, cords not pinched, and no candles left burning alone. Ask before you rearrange someone else's house. You don't need a huge display for it to feel festive.

topics.title: Holiday gatherings
topics.desc: At a holiday gathering, greet people, offer to help, put your phone away at the table if that's the house rule, and have a polite exit if you get overwhelmed. You don't have to debate every topic. A short thanks to the host when you leave is enough.

topics.title: Secret Santa
topics.desc: Secret Santa is a gift exchange where each person is assigned someone else to buy for, often with a spending limit. Keep the name quiet, stay in the budget, and pick something you'd be okay receiving. If you don't know the person well, a simple, useful gift or a gift card in the limit is fine.

topics.title: Mitosis and meiosis
topics.desc: Mitosis is ordinary cell division that makes two cells with the same number of chromosomes, used for growth and repair. Meiosis makes the sex cells, with half the usual chromosome number, so that a later joining can restore the full set. A class diagram of the stages helps more than memorizing names alone.

topics.title: Punnett squares
topics.desc: A Punnett square is a grid that shows possible allele combinations from two parents for a trait. Capital letters often mean a dominant allele, lowercase a recessive one, and each box is one possible offspring type. It shows chances, not a promise of what an actual child or plant will be.

topics.title: The rock cycle
topics.desc: The rock cycle describes how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks can change over time through melting, cooling, weathering, pressure and heat. A rock type is about how it formed, not a permanent label. A simple diagram of those paths is the usual class version.

topics.title: Climate versus weather
topics.desc: Weather is what's happening outside today: rain, wind, temperature. Climate is the longer pattern of weather in a place over many years. A cold week in a warm climate is still weather; a desert climate can still have a storm.

topics.title: Biomes
topics.desc: A biome is a large region with a characteristic climate and living things, such as a desert, tundra, rainforest, grassland or temperate forest. Plants and animals there have traits that fit that climate. A biome is bigger than one backyard ecosystem.

topics.title: The Cold War
topics.desc: The Cold War was a long period after World War II when the United States and the Soviet Union were rivals without fighting a direct full war against each other. It included an arms race, a space race, and proxy conflicts, and it eased as the Soviet Union ended in 1991. Details go deeper in class, but that's the basic frame.

topics.title: The Renaissance
topics.desc: The Renaissance was a period in Europe, starting in the later Middle Ages and flourishing in the 1400s and 1500s, known for renewed interest in art, science, learning and classical ideas. It didn't happen everywhere at once, and everyday life for many people still stayed hard. Artists and inventors from that time show up often in class.

topics.title: Supply and demand
topics.desc: Supply is how much of something sellers are willing to offer; demand is how much buyers want at a given price. When demand rises and supply stays tight, prices tend to go up; when there's more than people want, prices often fall. Real markets have other factors too, but that's the core idea.

topics.title: Opportunity cost
topics.desc: Opportunity cost is the next-best thing you give up when you choose something else, not only the price you pay. If you spend an afternoon at a job, the cost includes the time you didn't spend on homework or a friend. Thinking about it can make a choice clearer.

topics.title: Personification
topics.desc: Personification is a figure of speech that gives human qualities to something that isn't human, like a storm that 'rages' or a clock that 'watches.' Writers use it to make a scene feel alive. If a human is actually doing the action, it isn't personification.

topics.title: Alliteration
topics.desc: Alliteration is when nearby words start with the same sound, like 'wild wind' or 'big blue balloon.' Writers and advertisers use it because it's catchy. It is about the sound, not always the same letter, and one shared letter in a long sentence isn't automatically a strong example.

topics.title: The main idea
topics.desc: The main idea is the central point a passage is making, not every detail and not always the first sentence. Look at what most of the examples support, and try saying it in one sentence of your own. A title can hint, but the text itself is the evidence.

topics.title: Surface area
topics.desc: Surface area is the total area of the outside of a 3-D shape, like wrapping it. You add the areas of all the faces, using the right formula for each, and include units squared. A net of the shape can make the faces easier to see.

topics.title: Multiplying binomials
topics.desc: To multiply two binomials, such as (x + 2)(x + 5), you multiply each term in the first by each term in the second, then combine like terms. Some classes teach this as FOIL: first, outside, inside, last. The order of the four products doesn't matter as long as you don't skip one.

topics.title: Allowance
topics.desc: An allowance is money a family may give on a regular schedule. If you get one, a simple plan helps: some to spend, some to save, and sometimes some to give. Families handle this differently, and not getting an allowance doesn't mean you can't practice a budget with gift money or a job.

topics.title: A first paycheck
topics.desc: A first paycheck can look smaller than your hourly rate times hours because taxes and other deductions may come out first. Check your hours, the pay date, and how you'll be paid. Keep the stub, and ask a parent or the employer if a number looks wrong. I won't invent tax amounts.

topics.title: W-4 and a first job
topics.desc: A W-4 is a US form you fill out when you start a job so your employer can withhold federal income tax from your pay. Read it carefully, and ask a parent or the employer if a line is confusing. Filling it out honestly matters; I'm not a tax professional, so a tricky situation is worth adult help.

topics.title: Peer-to-peer payment apps
topics.desc: Apps that send money to friends are convenient, but they're not a game: only send to people you know, check the name twice, and treat the money as gone once it sends. Don't accept a payment you weren't expecting and then send it back to a stranger. Use a PIN or biometrics, and tell a parent if something looks like a scam.

topics.title: Impulse buying
topics.desc: Impulse buying is grabbing something you didn't plan to buy because it looked good in the moment. A short pause, a list, and a budget help. If it will still be there tomorrow, waiting a day is fair. You don't have to buy something just because it's on sale.

topics.title: Saving for a specific goal
topics.desc: Pick a goal, a target amount, and a realistic date, then divide so you know how much to set aside regularly. Keep that money separate if you can, and track small deposits so it feels real. If the date is tight, adjust the goal or the timeline instead of giving up. I won't invent prices; tell me the goal and I can help you plan.

topics.title: Buy now, pay later
topics.desc: Buy now, pay later splits a purchase into later payments, often with fees or a hard time if you miss one. If you couldn't pay for it soon anyway, it's a risky way to buy more than you can afford. Read the terms, and a regular purchase you can pay for now is usually simpler. I'm not a financial advisor, just a plain explanation.

topics.title: Splitting costs with friends
topics.desc: When you split a cost, agree up front who is paying, how you'll divide it, and how you'll settle, including tax and tip if it's a meal. Screenshots of the receipt help. If you can't afford your share, say so before the plan is locked, not after.

topics.title: A teen bank account
topics.desc: Many teen accounts need a parent or guardian as a joint or co-owner, and they can come with debit cards and limits. Compare fees, how you'll deposit money, and how you'll watch the balance. Ask the bank or credit union what they offer for your age; I won't invent their rules.

topics.title: Lending money to a friend
topics.desc: Only lend money you can afford not to get back, and be clear about whether it's a gift or a loan and when you'd like it back. A small amount is less likely to wreck a friendship than a large one. It's okay to say no. Don't borrow to lend.

topics.title: Turn signals
topics.desc: Use a turn signal before you turn or change lanes, early enough that other people can see it, and turn it off after. Signaling is how you tell others your plan, not optional decoration. Practice so it becomes automatic, even in a parking lot.

topics.title: Blind spots
topics.desc: A blind spot is an area beside or behind a car that your mirrors don't fully show. Quick shoulder checks, plus correctly aimed mirrors, help you catch a car or bike there before you change lanes. If you can't see past a large vehicle, give it more space and don't hang in that zone.

topics.title: Following distance
topics.desc: A common beginner rule is to leave about three seconds behind the vehicle in front: pick a marker, and you should reach it a few seconds after they do. Leave more space in rain, at night, or behind a large vehicle. Tailgating doesn't get you there sooner in a way that's worth the risk.

topics.title: Four-way stops
topics.desc: At a four-way stop, come to a full stop, then the first vehicle that stopped usually goes first. If two arrive together, the one on the right often has the right of way, and a person going straight may be yielded to by someone turning. Make eye contact when you can, and don't wave someone into a mess.

topics.title: Driving in the rain
topics.desc: In rain, slow down, leave more space, use headlights so others can see you, and avoid sudden steering or hard braking. If your car starts to hydroplane, ease off the gas and steer gently. Don't cruise through standing water when you can't judge the depth. Pull over safely if you can't see.

topics.title: Merging onto a highway
topics.desc: To merge, use the ramp to get close to highway speed, signal, look for a gap, and blend in rather than stopping at the end of the ramp unless traffic forces it. People already on the highway should also leave space when they can. Don't cut across several lanes the moment you're on.

topics.title: Night driving
topics.desc: At night, use headlights, slow down a little, and look to the right edge of the lane if an oncoming light is bright, not straight into it. Keep the windshield clean, and stay extra aware of pedestrians and animals. If you're tired, don't drive; sleepiness at night is a real risk.

topics.title: Getting pulled over
topics.desc: If a police car signals you to stop, pull over safely when you can, stay in the car unless you're told to get out, keep your hands visible, and wait to reach for your license or registration until you're asked. Be polite and don't argue on the roadside. A parent or guardian should hear about it afterward, and I'm not a lawyer.

topics.title: Changing lanes
topics.desc: To change lanes, signal, check mirrors and a blind-spot shoulder glance, then move over smoothly when there's space. Don't wander across a solid line just because you're in a hurry, and don't cut in tight. Cancel the signal after you're in the new lane.

topics.title: Choosing a pet
topics.desc: Choosing a pet should start with your time, budget, housing rules and how long that animal lives, not only how cute it is. Research the species, and talk with your family before you bring one home. A shelter can help you match a pet to your life. I won't invent costs; tell me your situation and I can help you think it through.

topics.title: Feeding a pet
topics.desc: Feed a pet the food and amount that fit its species, age and what a vet recommends, with fresh water available. Don't share a lot of human food, and keep chocolate, grapes, xylitol and other known dangers away from dogs. A sudden change in appetite is a reason to call the vet, not to guess online.

topics.title: Taking a pet to the vet
topics.desc: A vet visit is for checkups, shots and when something seems wrong. Bring a carrier or a secure leash, a list of what you've noticed, and, if you have it, the pet's records. Stay calm in the lobby if you can; your pet takes cues from you. The vet is the one who should diagnose, not a guess from a search.

topics.title: Signs a pet may be sick
topics.desc: Signs a pet may need a vet include not eating, vomiting more than once, trouble breathing, collapsing, a seizure, or being unusually hidden, weak or in pain. I'm not a vet and I won't diagnose from a chat. If you're worried, call the clinic or an emergency vet and tell a parent.

topics.title: Adopting from a shelter
topics.desc: A shelter or rescue can tell you about an animal's known history, temperament and needs, and often includes some starter vet care. Visit, ask questions, and be honest about your home and schedule. Adoption fees support the animals; I won't invent the amounts. Go with your family if a pet will live with all of you.

topics.title: Cat litter basics
topics.desc: A litter box should be scooped often, placed where the cat can reach it quietly, and kept in a number that matches how many cats you have, often one per cat plus one. A sudden change in bathroom habits can be a health issue, so call a vet instead of only scolding the cat. Wash your hands after cleaning.

topics.title: A new puppy
topics.desc: A new puppy needs a safe space, a feeding routine, potty breaks often, short training sessions, and sleep. Puppies chew, so keep dangerous items up. A vet visit, shots and a plan for crate or house training help early. It's work, and the cute stage is also a lot of supervision.

topics.title: Pet-proofing a room
topics.desc: Pet-proofing means moving chewable wires, small objects, toxic plants, medicines, and certain foods out of reach, and closing doors or using gates when you can't watch. Think from the animal's height. A little setup is easier than an emergency vet visit later.

topics.title: Fireworks and pets
topics.desc: Fireworks can scare pets. Ahead of a holiday, give them a quiet interior room, keep IDs on, don't take them to a show if they're fearful, and don't leave them in a yard unattended. If fear is extreme, ask a vet for a plan rather than guessing at medicine. Stay calm; it helps.

topics.title: The real cost of a pet
topics.desc: The cost of a pet is more than the first day: food, litter or waste bags, regular vet care, shots, a carrier or crate, and unexpected illness. Start with a family budget and an honest look at time. I won't invent prices; a shelter or vet can give local ranges, and I can help you list the categories.
